questions.q: Where should the main finding appear in a written analysis?
options: At the very end, after all the code
In an appendix
Nowhere; readers should discover it themselves
At the top, in a summary that stands alone
questions.explain: Readers want the answer first. Lead with it, then give the evidence for anyone who wants to check.

questions.q: Why format numbers into sentences with code instead of typing them by hand?
options: Because typed numbers are illegal in reports
So the text cannot drift out of sync with the data when you re-run the analysis
Because f-strings make the numbers larger
To hide the calculation from the reader
questions.explain: A common error is stale numbers after cleaning or re-running. Computed text updates with the data.

questions.q: The lesson's code printed '44.7% vs 11.3% with none (4.0x)'. What does 4.0x represent?
options: The ratio of churn rates: 44.7 divided by 11.3
The number of customers in the group
The number of tickets per customer
The difference between the two rates

questions.q: Which is NOT part of making an analysis reproducible?
options: Recording random seeds
Noting library versions
Running cells out of order until the answer looks right
Restarting and running all cells before sharing
questions.explain: A notebook that only works when cells run out of order is not reproducible.

questions.q: Why does the lesson stress reporting group sizes, such as the 103 customers with 3+ tickets?
options: A rate over a larger group is stronger evidence than the same rate over a very small one
Group sizes are required by pandas
It makes the chart look more colorful
Group size has no effect on how much to trust a rate
questions.explain: The same percentage rests on different amounts of evidence depending on how many customers are in the group.
